To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the power of panel unit root tests can be improved by removing incidental trends, and that the point optimal panel unit root test and Plogerger-Phillips test are both powerful in the sense of being uniformly most powerful.

the asymptotic power functions and the power envelope are obtained under the assumption of a common unit root process for all individuals in the panel, and that the power of the panel unit root tests depends on the incidental trends, which are extracted from the data.
the power envelope is obtained by the Ploberger–Phillips test under heterogeneous alternatives, and by the point optimal test under homogeneous alternatives.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the power of panel unit root tests.
the asymptotic power of various panel unit-root tests under homogeneous and heterogeneous local alternatives.
the power of tests for a unit root in the context of a panel of time series data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, under the assumption of homogeneous trends, the point optimal test is uniformly most powerful and the Ploberger Phillips test is uniformly most strict unbiased, while under the assumption of heterogeneous trends, the point optima tests and Ploberger Phillips tests are both asymptotically uniformly most powerful and uniformly most strict unbiased.
in the absence of incidental trends, the power envelope can be attained by the point optimal test.

the point optimal tests are uniformly most powerful in the sense of being uniformly most powerful in a neighborhood of unity that is of order n^{-\alpha}T^{-\beta} for some α, β > 0, and that the power envelope is achieved by the point optimal test in the homogeneous case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ploberger and Phillips (2002) and point optimal tests have the best performance in terms of power and size.
the power envelope of panel unit root tests is obtained by a point optimal test that does not extract incidental trends.
the power envelope is attained by a test that is a simple modification of the pooled t-statistic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ploberger–Phillips test and the point optimal test are both powerful against homogeneous alternatives.
, in the presence of incidental trends, it is important to use the point optimal test or Ploberger- Phillips test, which are more powerful than the pooled t-test.

when incidental trends are present, the power envelope of panel unit root tests is of order n^{-\alpha}T^{-\beta}, where \alpha and \beta are positive constants that depend on whether or not the alternative is homogeneous.
